My love of painting
by 15-year-old Kieron O’Driscoll
A
I enjoy all the usual things that other kids my age like doing – hanging out with
friends, going skateboarding and cycling. But I also spend time focusing on my
art, using different brushes and various kinds of paints to produce different
colours, and I try out a variety of techniques. I’ve even been fortunate enough to
show and sell my work through a gallery in my town and also at an arts festival in
the city, which runs for the whole of the month of May.
B
I wasn’t particularly into art when I was very young. I remember my parents
drawing dinosaurs and wildlife for me and I was happy to colour them in, but that
was as far as it went. It was during a family holiday to the seaside that I began
painting by myself. I was inspired by a harbour scene so I asked Mum and Dad for
some drawing paper. And that was it. I began painting the colourful boats on the
water and as the holiday went on, I began to add the background – like the tall
cliffs and some houses – to the picture.
C
I love painting landscapes – particularly ones with stormy skies and scenes that
show traditional farming methods – just like Edward Seago’s. He’s right at the
very top of my list when it comes to great painters. In fact, I live just down the road
from his house and I love knowing that he walked the same roads as me and
painted the same scenery. I find painting very relaxing and I almost forget about
everything else that’s going on around me. I finish each picture off by signing my
name and adding a tiny bird next to my signature.
D
No-one else in my family can paint, but my parents started to collect paintings by
local artists, like June Adamson, before I was born, so I’ve grown up with art on the
walls at home. I looked at them a lot. I particularly like one that’s hanging in the
living room, although I don't know who painted it. It’s of a nearby village. I think
that’s probably because I go there most weekends and enjoy the fields, the skies –
and even the smells! I’m hoping to do a picture of some cattle drinking at a stream. I
think it’ll look great, but I haven’t had the chance to start it yet.
Part 6
Questions 37–42
Read the text and questions below.
For each question, circle the correct letter: A, B, C or D.
Cheerleading
16-year-old Kerri talks about her hobby
When I was younger, I played ice hockey. I loved it, and had lots of friends on the team. One day, the
coach asked if I’d ever tried cheerleading. I thought that was a strange question, as I didn’t think the
two activities had anything in common. He explained that a local cheerleading team was looking for
new members, and he thought I might be good at it. I wasn’t sure, but I decided to try it.
The first time I went to a cheerleading practice, I felt quite nervous. The team were getting ready to do
their routine at a big football game. It had lots of amazing jumps and some really high lifts. I didn’t
think I could do those things, but I soon learned, and I was excited about preparing for the game. For
a while, I did both ice hockey and cheerleading, which meant four training sessions a week. One day,
I fell badly during an ice hockey match. The doctor told me that the reason I hadn’t really hurt myself
was because cheerleading had made my neck and shoulders quite strong.
In the USA, where I’m from, people are used to seeing cheerleaders at football matches. They’re
mostly girls, and they perform at the side of the field. Because they’re there to encourage the team
and entertain the crowd, people don’t think they’re serious athletes. However, cheerleaders train
incredibly hard, and many of them take part in competitions. To say that they’re not doing a proper
sport is very unfair.
You can learn a lot from cheerleading. If you're someone who's never been in a team before, you’ll
learn how to work with others, and make new friends too. Also, because cheerleading has so many
different routines, it’s great for your memory. That’s really helped me. Unfortunately, I still haven’t
learned how to arrive on time for practice!
The cheerleading team includes different types of people. Some are big and strong, while others are
smaller; some are very lively and confident, but others are quite shy, like me. What’s important is that
everyone knows exactly what to do, so that we can be certain that our teammates won’t drop us or fall
on us, and will know what the next move is.

16-year-old Kerri talks about her hobby

coach asked if I’d ever tried cheerleading. I thought that was a strange question, as I didn’t think the

new members, and he thought I might be good at it. I wasn’t sure, but I decided to try it.

think I could do those things, but I soon learned, and I was excited about preparing for the game. For

was because cheerleading had made my neck and shoulders quite strong.

everything else that’s going on around me. I finish each picture off by signing my
name and adding a tiny bird next to my signature.

local artists, like June Adamson, before I was born, so I’ve grown up with art on the
walls at home. I looked at them a lot. I particularly like one that’s hanging in the
living room, although I don't know who painted it. It’s of a nearby village. I think
that’s probably because I go there most weekends and enjoy the fields, the skies –
and even the smells! I’m hoping to do a picture of some cattle drinking at a stream. I
think it’ll look great, but I haven’t had the chance to start it yet.

For each question, circle the correct letter: A, B, C or D.
Cheerleading
16-year-old Kerri talks about her hobby
When I was younger, I played ice hockey. I loved it, and had lots of friends on the team. One day, the
coach asked if I’d ever tried cheerleading. I thought that was a strange question, as I didn’t think the
two activities had anything in common. He explained that a local cheerleading team was looking for
new members, and he thought I might be good at it. I wasn’t sure, but I decided to try it.
The first time I went to a cheerleading practice, I felt quite nervous. The team were getting ready to do
their routine at a big football game. It had lots of amazing jumps and some really high lifts. I didn’t
think I could do those things, but I soon learned, and I was excited about preparing for the game. For
a while, I did both ice hockey and cheerleading, which meant four training sessions a week. One day,
I fell badly during an ice hockey match. The doctor told me that the reason I hadn’t really hurt myself
was because cheerleading had made my neck and shoulders quite strong.
In the USA, where I’m from, people are used to seeing cheerleaders at football matches. They’re
mostly girls, and they perform at the side of the field. Because they’re there to encourage the team
and entertain the crowd, people don’t think they’re serious athletes. However, cheerleaders train
incredibly hard, and many of them take part in competitions. To say that they’re not doing a proper
sport is very unfair.
You can learn a lot from cheerleading. If you're someone who's never been in a team before, you’ll
learn how to work with others, and make new friends too. Also, because cheerleading has so many
different routines, it’s great for your memory. That’s really helped me. Unfortunately, I still haven’t
learned how to arrive on time for practice!
The cheerleading team includes different types of people. Some are big and strong, while others are
smaller; some are very lively and confident, but others are quite shy, like me. What’s important is that
everyone knows exactly what to do, so that we can be certain that our teammates won’t drop us or fall
on us, and will know what the next move is.

BMX, or bicycle motocross, is really popular where I live. The bikes are small and
strong so you can do jumps and other tricks on them. My cousin’s got one, and my

individual ones, which I’d say are better, as you get the coach’s full attention. It
seemed easy at first, so I decided to try a big jump – and ended up on the ground
with the bike on top of me! I guess I was too confident! I hope I can go again soon,
and I definitely want a BMX bike now.
B Maya
There’s a new skatepark in my town. It looks awesome, so I decided to have a
BMX lesson there. The coach, Harry, gave me my safety gear, and brought out the
bike. I couldn’t believe I had to ride something so small – I thought he’d given me a
bike for a little kid! Harry got me to do simple things at first, then gradually
introduced harder tricks, which was good, because I got less nervous the more I
did. The lesson was fun. I’d like to have another one if my parents agree.
C Tyler
I ride my bike a lot, but it’s not a BMX. I’d never been interested in that type of
cycling until my brother suggested booking a lesson with the BMX coach at our
local skatepark. I didn’t even know you could have BMX lessons there. I soon
discovered that you have to learn to jump and lift the whole bike off the ground
while you’re riding it. You can’t go on to do other things unless you can do that, and
unfortunately, I was really bad at it! I don’t think I’ll have another go – I’ll stick to my
road bike!
D Julia
My mum booked a BMX lesson for me because a friend said it was fun. I wanted to
try jumps immediately. But the coach, Sarah, needed to see what I could do on a
bike so she knew what to teach me, which made sense. And when I began going
down steeper hills, within a couple of minutes I was on my back and on the ground,
but I didn’t mind. Thanks to the safety gear, I wasn’t injured, and it’s good that it
happened at the beginning, because I learnt not to be afraid of hurting myself.

A review of The Wrong Wrights
13-year-old Arun talks about a graphic novel, which is a type of comic book
I’ve read a few graphic novels, although I’m not a big fan. My younger brother read one called The
Wrong Wrights, and showed me a review. It said ‘recommended for ages 9 to 12’. As I’m older than
that, I thought it’d be too young for me, but my brother went on about it so much, I decided to read it,
and I’m glad I did.
The main characters are four teenagers from the twenty-first century who travel back in time –
something I’d never seen in a book before. They go to 1903, when the Wright brothers invented the
aeroplane. Throughout the story, they discover more about planes and their inventors. Each teenager
has his or her own unique personality, although none is special in any way. That’s not a criticism. In
fact, I really love the fact that they’re quite normal. It means you can imagine yourself in the story.
As in all graphic novels, the story’s told through pictures with everyone’s words and thoughts in
speech bubbles. On a few pages there’s so much artwork that it looks quite confusing, even though
the artist’s drawings are quite simple, with lighter or darker colours used to show the different time
periods.
Two writers worked with the artist on the book, and after I’d read it, I watched a video interview with
one. I wanted to know whether he, like me, had visited the museum that appears in the book. He said
that visiting it had inspired him, and mentioned something I hadn’t realised – that this is the first of
several books they’re going to write together, each one based on a different museum. He also talked
about a feature I’d really enjoyed – the pages at the end that give the actual story of the Wrights. The
aim was to show that the writers changed some details – to make the book more fun, I guess.
Another interesting thing the author said was that many people we should know about are often
forgotten when history’s written down, like the Wrights’ sister Katharine, who actually gave her
brothers a lot of support. That’s why she was given a main role in The Wrong Wrights – so readers
will think about such forgotten men and women, and maybe try to find out more about them.

A review of The Wrong Wrights
13-year-old Arun talks about a graphic novel, which is a type of comic book
I’ve read a few graphic novels, although I’m not a big fan. My younger brother read one called The
Wrong Wrights, and showed me a review. It said ‘recommended for ages 9 to 12’. As I’m older than
that, I thought it’d be too young for me, but my brother went on about it so much, I decided to read it,
and I’m glad I did.
The main characters are four teenagers from the twenty-first century who travel back in time –
something I’d never seen in a book before. They go to 1903, when the Wright brothers invented the
aeroplane. Throughout the story, they discover more about planes and their inventors. Each teenager
has his or her own unique personality, although none is special in any way. That’s not a criticism. In
fact, I really love the fact that they’re quite normal. It means you can imagine yourself in the story.
As in all graphic novels, the story’s told through pictures with everyone’s words and thoughts in
speech bubbles. On a few pages there’s so much artwork that it looks quite confusing, even though
the artist’s drawings are quite simple, with lighter or darker colours used to show the different time
periods.
Two writers worked with the artist on the book, and after I’d read it, I watched a video interview with
one. I wanted to know whether he, like me, had visited the museum that appears in the book. He said
that visiting it had inspired him, and mentioned something I hadn’t realised – that this is the first of
several books they’re going to write together, each one based on a different museum. He also talked
about a feature I’d really enjoyed – the pages at the end that give the actual story of the Wrights. The
aim was to show that the writers changed some details – to make the book more fun, I guess.
Another interesting thing the author said was that many people we should know about are often
forgotten when history’s written down, like the Wrights’ sister Katharine, who actually gave her
brothers a lot of support. That’s why she was given a main role in The Wrong Wrights – so readers
will think about such forgotten men and women, and maybe try to find out more about them.

Film review of Catherine Called Birdy
by Nathan Stone, aged 14
A
Catherine Called Birdy is a film based on Karen Cushman’s very funny novel of the
same name. The main character is 14-year-old Catherine, who lives with her family
in thirteenth-century England. Because she loves birds, everyone calls her Birdy.
She enjoys running around the countryside having fun, and has no wish to grow
up, which is why she won’t accept the future her parents have planned for her. A
teenager rebelling against adults is an idea everyone’s probably heard before, but
that doesn’t mean that director Lena Dunham’s film isn’t worth watching. I left the
cinema still smiling to myself and singing the songs.
B
Although the film is set in the thirteenth century, it’s important to remember that the
way the characters speak is very different from the way people actually spoke at
that time, and Birdy is far more independent than a teenage girl would have been
back then. Bella Ramsey, who plays her, does it brilliantly because she’s just how I
imagined the character would be when I read the novel. Not everything in the film is
the way I thought it would be, however. Fans of Cushman’s writing may be
disappointed by the way Dunham has chosen to end it. To me it seemed an
unnecessary change.
C
Dunham, who has previously directed Tiny Furniture and Sharp Stick, probably
isn’t the first name you would think of to make a film set in medieval England, but
she’s kept to the spirit of the novel while making the film her own. Taking pop
songs and re-recording them to sound more like thirteenth-century music is an
interesting idea, and it mostly works well. It is also likely to be popular with
teenagers; after all, the film is mainly aimed at them.
D
Many of the roles in Catherine Called Birdy are played by well-known film stars,
and I thought they all gave excellent performances, with the exception of the one
who played Birdy’s uncle. I found him very difficult to understand, so I was glad he
wasn’t in it in many scenes. I’ve read some reviews of the film in which the
reviewers complain that the jokes don’t work. I don’t know which film they were
watching – I laughed all the way through!
Part 6

Read the text and questions below.
For each question, circle the correct letter: A, B, C or D.
Asha Kouri: a young designer making clothes from
recycled materials
When Asha was at design college, her teacher asked students to produce a range of clothes which
were environmentally friendly. Having attended several big music events with camping facilities, and
seeing the number of cheap, broken tents people couldn’t be bothered to take home with them, Asha
knew what she wanted to use in her design. After getting permission from an event organiser, she
collected old tents in greens, oranges and blues and took them home to wash and clean so they could
be made into clothes.
Some other students liked her idea and asked if she would mind if they did something similar. Rather
than being upset about her idea being copied, Asha realised that having others working with tent
material meant they could let each other know what worked and what didn’t. That would be a real
advantage, she said, as long as they didn’t produce the same items.
Asha aimed to use as much of the materials from the tents as possible. She began drawing skirt and
jacket designs on paper. Doing this before cutting the material helped her cut in the right places. And
actually, she only needed to buy a few extra buttons to fasten the skirt. She even used a tent zip for
the jacket!
Asha was given the third highest grade in her whole class for the project, and when she left college
soon after, she was offered a work placement for a year with famous designer Paul Jenson. He’s well
known for using traditional techniques to make modern clothing. Paul was supportive, letting Asha
make her designs on his machines. This was especially helpful as she was starting to sell more of her
clothes, although this was generally to friends and family.
Asha now has her own design business, which is growing, with the focus on using recycled material
for clothes for adults and recently for children. They are all made on her kitchen table and then sold in
her shop. From talking to customers, she’s realised people want to recycle clothes themselves. Asha
is about to advertise a course, which could be quite popular. This would give her the opportunity to
show others how to turn old clothes and items like sheets and blankets into stylish things to wear.

Film review of Catherine Called Birdy
by Nathan Stone, aged 14
A
Catherine Called Birdy is a film based on Karen Cushman’s very funny novel of the
same name. The main character is 14-year-old Catherine, who lives with her family

up, which is why she won’t accept the future her parents have planned for her. A
teenager rebelling against adults is an idea everyone’s probably heard before, but
that doesn’t mean that director Lena Dunham’s film isn’t worth watching. I left the
cinema still smiling to myself and singing the songs.

way the characters speak is very different from the way people actually spoke at
that time, and Birdy is far more independent than a teenage girl would have been
back then. Bella Ramsey, who plays her, does it brilliantly because she’s just how I
imagined the character would be when I read the novel. Not everything in the film is
the way I thought it would be, however. Fans of Cushman’s writing may be
disappointed by the way Dunham has chosen to end it. To me it seemed an
unnecessary change.

isn’t the first name you would think of to make a film set in medieval England, but

songs and re-recording them to sound more like thirteenth-century music is an
interesting idea, and it mostly works well. It is also likely to be popular with
teenagers; after all, the film is mainly aimed at them.
D

and I thought they all gave excellent performances, with the exception of the one
who played Birdy’s uncle. I found him very difficult to understand, so I was glad he
wasn’t in it in many scenes. I’ve read some reviews of the film in which the
reviewers complain that the jokes don’t work. I don’t know which film they were
watching – I laughed all the way through!

Asha Kouri: a young designer making clothes from
recycled materials
When Asha was at design college, her teacher asked students to produce a range of clothes which
were environmentally friendly. Having attended several big music events with camping facilities, and
seeing the number of cheap, broken tents people couldn’t be bothered to take home with them, Asha
knew what she wanted to use in her design. After getting permission from an event organiser, she
collected old tents in greens, oranges and blues and took them home to wash and clean so they could
be made into clothes.
Some other students liked her idea and asked if she would mind if they did something similar. Rather
than being upset about her idea being copied, Asha realised that having others working with tent
material meant they could let each other know what worked and what didn’t. That would be a real
advantage, she said, as long as they didn’t produce the same items.
Asha aimed to use as much of the materials from the tents as possible. She began drawing skirt and
jacket designs on paper. Doing this before cutting the material helped her cut in the right places. And
actually, she only needed to buy a few extra buttons to fasten the skirt. She even used a tent zip for
the jacket!
Asha was given the third highest grade in her whole class for the project, and when she left college
soon after, she was offered a work placement for a year with famous designer Paul Jenson. He’s well
known for using traditional techniques to make modern clothing. Paul was supportive, letting Asha
make her designs on his machines. This was especially helpful as she was starting to sell more of her
clothes, although this was generally to friends and family.
Asha now has her own design business, which is growing, with the focus on using recycled material
for clothes for adults and recently for children. They are all made on her kitchen table and then sold in
her shop. From talking to customers, she’s realised people want to recycle clothes themselves. Asha
is about to advertise a course, which could be quite popular. This would give her the opportunity to
show others how to turn old clothes and items like sheets and blankets into stylish things to wear.

fishing in Queensland, Australia. On a holiday to Tasmania, the brothers’ parents told surfers in the
area what the boys had found. Tasmania’s a small place, and local surfers wondered if it might be
Jamie’s missing board.
Jamie asked for photos of the board. Its green colour was familiar, and although the company brand
name had come off, its shape clearly indicated it was made by the small company from Tasmania
he’d used. He learned the brothers had hung it on their wall as a trophy. They did this because they
don’t surf, and anyway, it isn’t a surfboard many people could use – it’s built for riding huge waves.

caused by unusual weather conditions. According to experts, his surfboard didn’t take the most direct
route to Queensland, as that would have involved going against the movement of the water current.
So, it probably went a much longer and easier route along an eastern current into the Pacific Ocean,
before finally reaching the coast of Queensland.

wave, I fell off and was picked up on my friend’s jet ski. We looked everywhere, but my board had
disappeared. Nothing like this had ever happened to me. Looking after equipment is my top priority,
but it taught me that sometimes there’s nothing you can do.’ Jamie admits he misses the board. On a
recent surfing trip in Tasmania, he tried out a new one, but says the old one was far better.

travelling at high speeds. Experts told Jamie that sea creatures attached to the board would have
given information about where the board had been, but unfortunately the brothers had removed them.
Jamie thinks he might still be able to use the board. He’ll find out soon as the brothers are packing it
ready to send.

A review of the film The First Slam Dunk
Henry Slate, aged 14, reviews an animated film which was based on
a comic book series and a TV series.
A
The original Slam Dunk was a Japanese manga – that’s a kind of comic book –
which told the story of a school basketball team. It was later made into an incredibly
successful TV series, which ended nearly thirty years ago. The animated film
version The First Slam Dunk continues the team’s story, focusing on one important
game. However, instead of the game happening at the end, we see parts of it
throughout the film as we find out about each character’s life. This makes for an
exciting film, although there’s only time for audiences to get a complete picture of
two or three main players rather than all of them, which is a real pity.
B
In the original TV series, the star of the show was red-haired Hanamichi Sakuragi,
whereas in The First Slam Dunk we see and hear much more about another
player, Ryota Miyagi, who I’m sure audiences will love, as I did. As time goes on,
we find out more about why each boy started playing; in other words, by the end of
the film, they feel like actual people rather than simply animations. There’s also the
added bonus that you could enter the cinema knowing nothing about the sport and
leave it talking about free throws and chest passes like an expert.

three-dimensional images, and the effect is like nothing I’ve ever seen before. The
characters look incredibly realistic in the way they move – sometimes it’s hard to
believe they’re not real people. And because the players look so real, the audience
members become completely involved in the on-screen basketball game. Directors
often create atmosphere using music and other background noises, but it was the
use of silence to build tension through some of the game that was really clever and
original in this film.
D
Of course, as in almost every other sports film, our team of heroes eventually
wins their game in the final scene. Personally, I was really hoping for something
a little less obvious, but this didn’t stop me from loving the rest of The First Slam
Dunk. For fans of the original Slam Dunk series, it brings the team’s story to a
close. Although those who are less familiar with the characters may find it hard
to understand their relationships at times, it’s a great introduction to the graphic
stories and the classic TV programme. I’m sure they’ll want to see both after
this film.

My travels
By Iqbal Hussain, aged 11
Eighteen months ago, my parents started a two-year-long trip around the world,
taking me with them. We’re travelling in a motorhome, a sort of large van that
you can live in, which has everything we need. Sure, we have less space than
in our house, but we’ve got the whole world to explore. What more could you
ask for? It’s great that I’ve been allowed to go away for so long!
I still have to do schoolwork, but my mum teaches me, and I manage well
because I’m also able to contact my teachers, if we have wi-fi, of course. They
ask me to describe the places I visit by making up stories about them, which I
like. And what’s really great is studying by doing all sorts of unusual things, for
example, watching wild animals or photographing them.
We spent some time in southern Africa, in the Kalahari Desert, and went on a
tour one evening to look at the night sky. As deserts get so dark, they’re
wonderful places to see thousands of stars, and our guide, Ivan, told us some
of their names. We were a long way from anywhere and I couldn’t believe that
there was no noise at all. But it was so cold when we were there, I was glad I
had a big coat on.
When we went to South Africa, we took a boat trip and saw some whales. I
liked them. They reminded me of us on our travels, because just like me, the
young whales are very rarely away from their parents. Something I learnt later
was that the mothers keep their young in front of them as they swim, so that
they’re safe. It seems they swim all the way to the icy seas of Antarctica. In
fact, they spend a lot of time travelling.

Part 6
Questions 30–34
Read the text below and the questions on the opposite page.
For each question, circle the correct letter: A, B or C.
The board game café
11-year-old Pierre visits a café where people go to play board games.
My family often play a board game called Storyboard. Someone tells a story and
the others ask loads of questions and discuss whether they think the story’s true,
so it gets really noisy. Games like that are my favourite, but ones where it’s
important to think carefully and remember stuff are great too. I often beat my dad
at chess, for example. I enjoy deciding what my next moves will be.
Last weekend, my family and I visited a new board-game café. As we entered, I
thought: ‘This is cool!’ It had two big rooms full of people playing games, with
everyone laughing and having a good time. We waited ages for a free table. I
never knew people liked board games so much.
There were hundreds of games to choose from. A waiter suggested one called
Brightside that we hadn’t played before. He said it only took an hour to play, and
then we could try another one – we decided that was excellent advice. When we
started playing, we found it had simple rules and was great fun.
We decided to eat something before our next game. The menu had the usual
things – pizza, sandwiches and cake, which was good. Everything was really
expensive but we all shared a cake. The top was like a chess board, with black
and white chocolate squares. It looked a bit strange, but it was delicious.
Before we left, I chatted to someone who was working there. She said there would
be competitions later in the year, and lots of young players like me would come.
She asked if I was interested in entering them. Of course I am. So, she told me to
phone the café and speak to the manager there to get more information.

socially, but everyone uses technology to communicate now, so programming is
considered cool. I’ve got lots of friends who are into computer science and want
careers as programmers. They want to work for big tech companies as they

for people with plenty of self-confidence! He found cycling around the area dull compared with the
surfing he’d enjoyed so much. When his new friends told him that the mountains, a short distance
away by car, were perfect for snowboarding, he hoped it might provide that same excitement again.

instructor. The other snowboarders on the slopes were friendly, constantly giving advice. While this
was kind, Samir realised that concentrating just on what his friend was saying was far simpler. He
also found moving on snow surprisingly easy, and the slope wasn’t steep, so he had no worries about
injuries.

as skis were easier to control. Samir was willing to try it, but couldn’t wait to get back on his
snowboard because he loves the fact that he’s always improving, and it’s where he feels most at

sportswear shop, and he’s now receiving free snowboarding gear for twelve months! People seemed

events.

anyone snowboard? Samir says, ‘Being on the mountain takes energy. But even people who aren’t
particularly fit can manage beginners’ lessons, so go for it!’

Samir Badri: young snowboarder
As a child, 15-year-old Samir lived by the coast, where he loved surfing. Then, his family moved away
from the sea to a big city. Initially, Samir was busy settling into a new school, which isn’t easy, even
for people with plenty of self-confidence! He found cycling around the area dull compared with the
surfing he’d enjoyed so much. When his new friends told him that the mountains, a short distance
away by car, were perfect for snowboarding, he hoped it might provide that same excitement again.
Samir’s friend offered to teach him to snowboard, rather than him having to find a professional
instructor. The other snowboarders on the slopes were friendly, constantly giving advice. While this
was kind, Samir realised that concentrating just on what his friend was saying was far simpler. He
also found moving on snow surprisingly easy, and the slope wasn’t steep, so he had no worries about
injuries.
When he first started snowboarding, people said he should try skiing instead, explaining it was safer
as skis were easier to control. Samir was willing to try it, but couldn’t wait to get back on his
snowboard because he loves the fact that he’s always improving, and it’s where he feels most at
home.
Nowadays, Samir’s entering snowboarding competitions. The latest one was on a challenging course
where the national team trains. Samir read articles about these snowboarders for tips, and before the
event, he had special race lessons, which paid off, as he won! The race was sponsored by a
sportswear shop, and he’s now receiving free snowboarding gear for twelve months! People seemed
interested in how he had prepared, so he set up a blog for them to follow his progress at future
events.
When asked about future races, Samir explains, ‘Snowboarding’s competitive, but I’ve got as much
chance as anyone!’ Snowboarding’s changed Samir’s life in unexpected ways. For example, he’s now
great at time management. Schoolwork gets done before he heads to the mountains, which he does
at least twice a week. He also loves that snowboarding has its own fashion and music. So, can
anyone snowboard? Samir says, ‘Being on the mountain takes energy. But even people who aren’t
particularly fit can manage beginners’ lessons, so go for it!’

Programming computers
Four teenagers talk about their hobby
A Olivier
A couple of years ago, I wanted to join a science club because I wanted to do
experiments. The teacher said I was too young and suggested a computer
programming club instead. I’ve loved it ever since. When my parents were
younger, there was this idea that programmers were lonely and never mixed
socially, but everyone uses technology to communicate now, so programming is
considered cool. I’ve got lots of friends who are into computer science and want
careers as programmers. They want to work for big tech companies as they
provide really cool working spaces and offices for all their employees.
B Luna
When I was little, I desperately wanted to draw, but I was useless at it, so my dad,
who works as a programmer, showed me how to use a computer to make shapes
and animations, and I thought it was brilliant. I didn’t even realise at the time that I
was programming. I played around with Dad’s old laptop so much that it was
always getting viruses. It stopped working completely in the end. I’m more careful
now, though. I'm designing a website about Japanese animation at the moment.
I can’t decide whether to show it to my friends yet because I’m nervous about
their reactions.
C Jai
My parents are quite strict and wouldn’t let me and my brothers buy computer
games, so I decided to design my own, which involved programming. I’ve made a
few now, and right now I’m working on one that you can play if you’re blind. Most
games aren’t designed for those players, so they miss out, and that’s obviously
not fair. I love the fact that, with programming, you’re always learning something
new. One day, I want to come up with a game or a type of computer that no one
has ever thought of before.
D Hassan
What I find really fun about programming is experimenting and seeing what you
can come up with. For example, when I stopped going to the gym, I took my
electronic membership card and programmed it to turn on the lights in my
bedroom. I’ve done that kind of thing since I was quite young. And even though I
spend money on games, I don’t really play them like other people. Instead, I find
ways of changing them to make them more challenging or more entertaining. I
find it quite surprising that, unlike me, many of my classmates don’t enjoy
programming.

Programming computers
Four teenagers talk about their hobby
A Olivier
A couple of years ago, I wanted to join a science club because I wanted to do
experiments. The teacher said I was too young and suggested a computer
programming club instead. I’ve loved it ever since. When my parents were
younger, there was this idea that programmers were lonely and never mixed
socially, but everyone uses technology to communicate now, so programming is
considered cool. I’ve got lots of friends who are into computer science and want
careers as programmers. They want to work for big tech companies as they
provide really cool working spaces and offices for all their employees.
B Luna
When I was little, I desperately wanted to draw, but I was useless at it, so my dad,
who works as a programmer, showed me how to use a computer to make shapes
and animations, and I thought it was brilliant. I didn’t even realise at the time that I
was programming. I played around with Dad’s old laptop so much that it was
always getting viruses. It stopped working completely in the end. I’m more careful
now, though. I'm designing a website about Japanese animation at the moment.
I can’t decide whether to show it to my friends yet because I’m nervous about
their reactions.
C Jai
My parents are quite strict and wouldn’t let me and my brothers buy computer
games, so I decided to design my own, which involved programming. I’ve made a
few now, and right now I’m working on one that you can play if you’re blind. Most
games aren’t designed for those players, so they miss out, and that’s obviously
not fair. I love the fact that, with programming, you’re always learning something
new. One day, I want to come up with a game or a type of computer that no one
has ever thought of before.
D Hassan
What I find really fun about programming is experimenting and seeing what you
can come up with. For example, when I stopped going to the gym, I took my
electronic membership card and programmed it to turn on the lights in my
bedroom. I’ve done that kind of thing since I was quite young. And even though I
spend money on games, I don’t really play them like other people. Instead, I find
ways of changing them to make them more challenging or more entertaining. I
find it quite surprising that, unlike me, many of my classmates don’t enjoy
programming.
Part 6
Questions 37–42
Read the text and questions below.
For each question, circle the correct letter: A, B, C or D.
Samir Badri: young snowboarder
As a child, 15-year-old Samir lived by the coast, where he loved surfing. Then, his family moved away
from the sea to a big city. Initially, Samir was busy settling into a new school, which isn’t easy, even
for people with plenty of self-confidence! He found cycling around the area dull compared with the
surfing he’d enjoyed so much. When his new friends told him that the mountains, a short distance
away by car, were perfect for snowboarding, he hoped it might provide that same excitement again.
Samir’s friend offered to teach him to snowboard, rather than him having to find a professional
instructor. The other snowboarders on the slopes were friendly, constantly giving advice. While this
was kind, Samir realised that concentrating just on what his friend was saying was far simpler. He
also found moving on snow surprisingly easy, and the slope wasn’t steep, so he had no worries about
injuries.
When he first started snowboarding, people said he should try skiing instead, explaining it was safer
as skis were easier to control. Samir was willing to try it, but couldn’t wait to get back on his
snowboard because he loves the fact that he’s always improving, and it’s where he feels most at
home.
Nowadays, Samir’s entering snowboarding competitions. The latest one was on a challenging course
where the national team trains. Samir read articles about these snowboarders for tips, and before the
event, he had special race lessons, which paid off, as he won! The race was sponsored by a
sportswear shop, and he’s now receiving free snowboarding gear for twelve months! People seemed
interested in how he had prepared, so he set up a blog for them to follow his progress at future
events.
When asked about future races, Samir explains, ‘Snowboarding’s competitive, but I’ve got as much
chance as anyone!’ Snowboarding’s changed Samir’s life in unexpected ways. For example, he’s now
great at time management. Schoolwork gets done before he heads to the mountains, which he does
at least twice a week. He also loves that snowboarding has its own fashion and music. So, can
anyone snowboard? Samir says, ‘Being on the mountain takes energy. But even people who aren’t
particularly fit can manage beginners’ lessons, so go for it!’
